info.desc: Young Americans is the ninth studio album by David Bowie, released on March 7, 1975, through RCA Records. Marking a departure from his glam rock style, the album explores soul and R&B, with Bowie describing it as "plastic soul". It features contributions from Carlos Alomar, Luther Vandross, and a collaboration with John Lennon on "Fame" (Bowie's first U.S. #1 hit) and a cover of "Across the Universe". Recorded at Sigma Sound Studios in Philadelphia and the Record Plant in New York, the album reflects Bowie's growing interest in American black music, influenced by artists like Aretha Franklin. podcast.body: During the recording of this album, David Bowie entered a peculiar phase characterized by continuous changes in his entourage, including managers and close team members, and problems with his wife. He also began a period of constant changes in residence, indicating he was already becoming "out of control" despite his creative output remaining interesting and good. "Ya durante la grabación de John Americans, David Bowie entra en una fase entanto extraña en la que tiene continuos cambios de personas que le rodean, hay varios cambios de manajera, hay varios cambios de personas de su equipo de cercanía, tiene problemas con su mujer y además se empieza en una etapa de continuos cambios de residencia."

podcast.body: Recorded in Philadelphia and New York City, this 1975 album was a significant stylistic pivot, with Bowie fully committing to what he called "Plastic Soul," delving deep into American R&B. The album immediately cracked the top 10, reaching number 9, and featured collaborators like Carlos Alomar, David Sanborn, and Luther Vandross. "Young Americans remains one of the great stylistic pivots by any artist in rock history. Boey fully committed to what he called Plastic Soul, going deep on his love of American R&B for the first time since the mid-60s."

podcast.body: Released on March 7, 1975, this album marked the debut of yet another Bowie persona: the "blue-eyed plastic soul singer." It was his sixth album in three years and two months. The album showcased Bowie's new interest in American soul and R&B, featuring a smoother, funkier sound developed during studio breaks on the "Diamond Dogs" tour. "Young Americans introduced yet another Bowie. The blue-eyed plastic soul singer."

podcast.body: This album marked a period in Bowie's career where songs and albums were released continuously. Over approximately three years, Bowie released six albums during this "imperial phase." "Bowie was still in his imperial phase. That part of his career where the songs and albums just kept coming."
